English translation:
1 Antonius Heronianus, horseman of the cohort [I Lusi]-
2 ta[no]r[um], troop of Marianus, to Julius Ser[enus] [...],
3 hor[seman of the same cohort], greeting in good faith. [I acknowledge that I] [...]
4 have received [and] owe seventy-[nine] silver denarii,
5 which I will repay you when my pay is received [...]
6 with in[terest], or to your agent or heir [...].
7 Julius Serenus, horseman, stipulated; [Antonius Heronianus]
8 promised for LX[XIX] silver denarii [...]
9 of the day written below. Done at the fort Net[...] in the detach-
10 ment of the cohort written above, on the 6th day before the Ides of August, [when Imperator Antoninus]
11 Augustus Pius for the 3rd time and Aurelius Caesar, [son of] Au[gustus Pius, were consuls].
12 I, Antonius Heronianus, [have received] [79 silver denarii]
13 as a lo[a]n and will re[pay as aforesaid].

Latin, with a Greek subscription calling it a loan (δανεισμόν, l. 13); both parties are horsemen of the cohort I Lusitanorum; the sum, partly restored in Latin, is written in full in the Greek (l. 13).
Interest: "with in[terest]" (cum us[uris], l. 6), mostly restored; no rate.
Term: when the borrower's pay is received (l. 5).
Date: 6th day before the Ides of August, consulship of Antoninus Pius (3rd) and Marcus Aurelius Caesar (= 8 August AD 140).
Place: done at the fort Net[...] (l. 9); the tablet was found at Karanis (HGV).

Original Text:
10 habes consilia nostra; nunc cognosce de Bruto. familiaris habet Brutus tuus quosdam creditores Salaminiorum ex Cypro, M. Scaptium et P. Matinium; quos mihi maiorem in modum commendavit. Matinium non novi, Scaptius ad me in castra venit. pollicitus sum curaturum me Bruti causa ut ei Salaminii pecuniam solverent. egit gratias. praefecturam petivit. negavi me cuiquam negotianti dare (quod idem tibi ostenderam Cn. Pompeio petenti probaram institutum meum, quid dicam Torquato de M. Laenio tuo, multis aliis?); sin praefectus vellet esse syngraphae causa, me curaturum ut exigeret. gratias egit, discessit. Appius noster turmas aliquot equitum dederat huic Scaptio per quas Salaminios coerceret, et eundem habuerat praefectum; vexabat Salaminios. ego equites ex Cypro decedere iussi. moleste tulit Scaptius.
11 quid multa? ut ei fidem meam praestarem, cum ad me Salaminii Tarsum venissent et in iis Scaptius, imperavi ut pecuniam solverent. multa de syngrapha, de Scapti iniuriis. negavi me audire; hortatus sum, petivi etiam pro meis in civitatem beneficiis ut negotium conficerent, dixi denique me coacturum. homines non modo non recusare sed etiam hoc dicere, se a me solvere. quod enim praetori dare consuessent, quoniam ego non acceperam, se a me quodam modo dare atque etiam minus esse aliquanto in Scapti nomine quam in vectigali praetorio. conlaudavi homines. recte inquit Scaptius, sed subducamus summam. interim cum ego in edicto translaticio centesimas me observaturum haberem cum anatocismo anniversario, ille ex syngrapha postulabat quaternas. quid ais? inquam, possumne contra meum edictum? at ille profert senatus consultum Lentulo Philippoque consulibus, ut qui Ciliciam obtineret ius ex illa sungrapha diceret.
12 cohorrui primo; etenim erat interitus civitatis. reperio duo senatus consulta isdem consulibus de eadem syngrapha. Salaminii cum Romae versuram facere vellent, non poterant, quod lex Gabinia vetabat. tum iis Bruti familiares freti gratia Bruti dare volebant quaternis, si sibi senatus consulto caveretur. fit gratia Bruti senatus consultum, ut neve salaminis neve qui eis dedisset fraudi esset. pecuniam numerarunt. at postea venit in mentem faeneratoribus nihil se iuvare illud senatus consultum, quod ex syngrapha ius dici lex Gabinia vetaret. tum fit senatus consultum, ut ex ea syngrapha ius diceretur, non ut alio iure ea syngrapha esset quam ceterae sed ut eodem. cum haec disseruissem, seducit me Scaptius; ait se nihil contra dicere sed illos putare talenta cc se debere; ea se velle accipere; debere autem illos paulo minus. rogat ut eos ad ducenta perducam. optime inquam. voco illos ad me remoto Scaptio. quid? vos quantum inquam debetis? respondent cvi. refero ad Scaptium. homo clamare. quid? opus est inquam rationes conferatis. adsidunt, subducunt; ad nummum convenit. illi se numerare velle, urgere ut acciperet. Scaptius me rursus seducit, rogat ut rem sic relinquam. dedi veniam homini impudenter petenti; Graecis querentibus, ut in fano deponerent postulantibus non concessi. clamare omnes qui aderant, alii nihil impudentius Scaptio qui centesimis cum anatocismo contentus non esset, alii nihil stultius. mihi autem impudens magis quam stultus videbatur; nam aut bono nomine centesimis contentus non erat aut non bono quaternas centesimas sperabat. habes meam causam.

English translation:
10 You have my plans; now hear about Brutus. Your friend Brutus has as close friends certain creditors of the Salaminians of Cyprus, Marcus Scaptius and Publius Matinius, whom he commended to me in the strongest terms. Matinius I do not know; Scaptius came to me in camp. I promised that for Brutus' sake I would see that the Salaminians paid him the money. He thanked me. He asked for a prefecture. I said that I gave one to no man in business (as I had shown you too; I had made Gnaeus Pompeius accept my rule when he asked, and what shall I say of Torquatus about your Marcus Laenius, and many others?); but if he wanted to be prefect for the sake of the bond, I would see that he collected it. He thanked me and left. Our friend Appius had given this Scaptius some troops of cavalry with which to coerce the Salaminians, and had had him as prefect; he was harassing the Salaminians. I ordered the cavalry to leave Cyprus. Scaptius took it badly.
11 In short: to keep my word to him, when the Salaminians came to me at Tarsus, and Scaptius with them, I ordered them to pay the money. Much was said about the bond and about Scaptius' wrongs. I refused to listen; I urged them, I even asked them in return for my kindnesses to their city to settle the business; finally I said I would compel them. The men not only did not refuse but said that they were paying out of my pocket: for what they used to give the governor, since I had not taken it, they were in a way giving out of mine, and the amount on Scaptius' claim was even somewhat less than the governor's levy. I praised them. "Very well," says Scaptius, "but let us add up the sum." Meanwhile, whereas in my edict, following the standard one, I had said that I would observe interest of one per cent a month with yearly compounding, he demanded four per cent under the bond. "What do you say?" said I; "can I go against my own edict?" But he produces a decree of the senate of the consulship of Lentulus and Philippus, that whoever governed Cilicia should give judgment on the basis of that bond.
12 At first I shuddered; for it meant the ruin of the city. I find two decrees of the senate of the same consuls on the same bond. When the Salaminians wished to raise a loan at Rome, they could not, because the Gabinian law forbade it. Then Brutus' friends, relying on Brutus' influence, were willing to lend to them at four per cent a month, if they were secured by a decree of the senate. Through Brutus' influence a decree of the senate is passed, that neither the Salaminians nor whoever had lent to them should be liable. They counted out the money. But afterwards it occurred to the moneylenders that that decree did not help them, because the Gabinian law forbade judgment to be given on such a bond. Then a decree of the senate is passed that judgment be given on that bond, not so that the bond should have different rights from all others, but the same. When I had explained this, Scaptius takes me aside; he says that he does not dispute it, but they think they owe 200 talents; he wishes to receive that; but they owe a little less. He asks me to bring them up to two hundred. "Very well," I say. I call them in, Scaptius being sent away. "Well, how much do you owe?" I ask. They answer: 106. I report it to Scaptius. The man shouted. "Well," I say, "you must compare your accounts." They sit down and add up; it agrees to the sesterce. They say they wish to pay, they press him to accept. Scaptius takes me aside again and asks me to leave the matter so. I granted the request of a man asking shamelessly; when the Greeks complained and demanded to deposit the money in a temple, I did not allow it. All who were present cried out, some that nothing was more shameless than Scaptius, who was not content with one per cent with compound interest, others that nothing was more foolish. To me he seemed shameless rather than foolish; for either on a good debt he was not content with one per cent, or on a bad one he was hoping for four. There you have my case.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
The Salaminians of Cyprus borrowed at Rome from Scaptius and Matinius, friends of Marcus Brutus, under a bond (syngrapha), with two decrees of the senate to get round the Gabinian law (§12); Cicero, governor of Cilicia, met the parties at Tarsus in 50 BC (§11). The principal is not given: in 50 BC Scaptius claimed 200 talents, the Salaminians reckoned 106 (§12). Cicero tells the story again in Att. 6.1.5-7, 6.2.7-9 and 6.3.5.
Interest: four per cent a month under the bond (quaternae, §§11-12); Cicero's edict allowed one per cent a month with yearly compounding.
Date: the loan was made under the consuls Lentulus and Philippus (§11), i.e. 56 BC; the letter is of 50 BC.
Place: borrowed at Rome (§12).

Original text: Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum, ed. L. C. Purser (Oxford 1903); Perseus Digital Library (canonical-latinLit), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Original Text:
3 nunc venio ad Brutum quem ego omni studio te auctore sum complexus, quem etiam amare coeperam; sed ilico me revocavi, ne te offenderem. noli enim putare me quicquam maluisse quam ut mandatis satis facerem nec ulla de re plus laborasse. mandatorum autem mihi libellum dedit, isdemque de rebus tu mecum egeras. omnia sum diligentissime persecutus. primum ab Ariobarzane sic contendi ut talenta quae mihi pollicebatur illi daret. quoad mecum rex fuit, perbono loco res erat; post a Pompei procuratoribus sescentis premi coeptus est. Pompeius autem quom ob ceteras causas plus potest unus quam ceteri omnes, tum quod putatur ad bellum Parthicum esse venturus. ei tamen sic nunc solvitur, tricesimo quoque die talenta Attica xxxiii et hoc ex tributis. nec inde satis efficitur in usuram menstruam. sed Gnaeus noster clementer id fert; sorte caret, usura nec ea solida contentus est. alii neque solvit cuiquam nec potest solvere; nullum enim aerarium, nullum vectigal habet. Appi instituto tributa imperat. ea vix in faenus Pompei quod satis sit efficiunt. amici regis duo tresve perdivites sunt sed ii suum tam diligenter tenent quam ego aut tu. equidem non desino tamen per litteras rogare, suadere, accusare regem.

English translation:
3 Now I come to Brutus, whom on your advice I embraced with all zeal, whom I had even begun to love; but at once I checked myself, so as not to offend you. Do not think that I wished for anything more than to carry out your commissions, or took more trouble over anything. He gave me a list of commissions, and you had discussed the same matters with me. I have pursued them all most diligently. First I pressed Ariobarzanes to give him the talents he was promising me. As long as the king was with me, the matter stood very well; afterwards he began to be pressed by Pompeius' agents, six hundred of them. And Pompeius, both for other reasons can do more alone than all the rest, and because he is thought to be coming to the Parthian war. Yet he is now being paid in this way: every thirtieth day thirty-three Attic talents, and that out of taxes. Nor is that enough for the monthly interest. But our Gnaeus bears it mildly; he goes without the principal, and is content with the interest, and not even that in full. To anyone else he neither pays nor can pay; for he has no treasury, no revenue. He levies taxes on the system of Appius; they barely produce enough for Pompeius' interest. The king's friends, two or three, are very rich, but they keep hold of their own as carefully as you or I. For my part I do not stop asking, urging and reproaching the king by letter.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Pompeius' loan to King Ariobarzanes of Cappadocia: the king pays 33 Attic talents every thirty days out of taxes, which does not cover the monthly interest; Pompeius forgoes the principal (sors) for now. The king's debt to Brutus, in the same passage, is not called a loan (need_review.md).
Interest: monthly interest (usura menstrua), not covered by the payments; no rate.
Date: not stated; the year of the letter (Laodicea, 50 BC); the loan was made earlier.

Original Text:
2 illa de ratione nummaria non sunt eius modi (saepe enim audio ex ipso) ut non cupiat tibi praestare et in eo laboret. sed si mihi Q. Axius in hac mea fuga HS ⅹ̅ⅰ̅ⅰ̅ⅰ̅ non reddit quae dedi eius filio mutua et utitur excusatione temporis, si Lepta, si ceteri, soleo mirari de nescio quis HS ⅹ̅ⅹ̅ cum audio ex illo se urgeri. vides enim profecto angustias. curari tamen ea tibi utique iubet. an existimas illum in isto genere lentulum aut restrictum? nemo est minus.

English translation:
2 Those matters of money are not such (I often hear it from him) that he does not wish to make good to you and take trouble over it. But if Quintus Axius does not return to me in this flight of mine the 13,000 sesterces which I lent his son, and pleads the times as an excuse, if Lepta, if the others, I am apt to wonder about some 20,000 sesterces or so when I hear from him that he is being pressed. For you surely see the straits. Yet he orders that it be seen to for you in any case. Or do you think him slow or close in such matters? No one is less so.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Cicero complains that Quintus Axius does not repay the 13,000 sesterces Cicero lent his son; in Att. 10.15.4 the sum is twelve thousand.
Date: not stated; the year of the letter (Cumae, 49 BC); the loan was made earlier.

Original Text:
3 pecunia apud Egnatium est. sit a me ut est. neque enim hoc quod agitur videtur diuturnum esse posse, ut scire iam possim quid maxime opus sit; etsi egeo rebus omnibus, quod is quoque in angustiis est quicum sumus; cui magnam dedimus pecuniam mutuam opinantes nobis constitutis rebus eam rem etiam honori fore. tu ut antea fecisti, velim si qui erunt ad quos aliquid scribendum a me existimes ipse conficias. tuis salutem dic. cura ut valeas. in primis id quod scribis omnibus rebus cura et provide ne quid ei desit de qua scis me miserrimum esse. Idibus Iuniis ex castris.

English translation:
3 The money is with Egnatius. Let it stay as it is. For this state of affairs does not seem able to last long, so that I may soon know what is most needed; although I lack everything, because he too with whom we are is in straits; to whom we lent a large sum of money, thinking that when things were settled it would also bring us credit. Please, as you did before, if there are any to whom you think I should write, do it yourself. Give my greetings to your family. Take care of your health. Above all, as you write, take care and see in every way that she whom you know I am most anxious about lacks nothing. On the Ides of June, from the camp.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
"He with whom we are" is Pompeius, in whose camp Cicero writes during the civil war; Cicero lent him a large sum. In Att. 11.13.4 Cicero says he handed over all his means to Pompeius.
Date: written in the camp on the Ides of June (13 June 48 BC); the loan was made shortly before.

Original text: Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum, ed. L. C. Purser (Oxford 1903); Perseus Digital Library (canonical-latinLit), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Original Text:
4 de fundo Frusinati redimendo iam pridem intellexisti voluntatem meam. etsi tum meliore loco res erant nostrae neque tam mihi desperatum iri videbatur, tamen in eadem sum voluntate. id quem ad modum fiat tu videbis. et velim, quod poteris, consideres ut sit unde nobis suppeditentur sumptus necessarii. si quas habuimus facultates, eas Pompeio tum cum id videbamur sapienter facere detulimus. itaque tum et a tuo vilico sumpsimus et aliunde mutuati sumus cum Quintus queritur per litteras sibi nos nihil dedisse, qui neque ab illo rogati sumus neque ipsi eam pecuniam aspeximus. sed velim videas quid sit quod confici possit quidque mihi de omnibus des consili; et causam nosti.

English translation:
4 About redeeming the farm at Frusino you have long understood my wish. Although our affairs were then in a better state and it did not seem to me that things would become so desperate, yet I am of the same mind. How it is to be done you will see. And please consider, as far as you can, where the necessary expenses can be supplied to us from. Whatever means we had, we handed over to Pompeius at the time when we seemed to be acting wisely. So at that time we both took from your bailiff and borrowed from elsewhere, while Quintus complains by letter that we gave him nothing, though we were not asked by him nor did we ourselves see that money. But please see what can be arranged and give me your advice on everything; and you know the case.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
When Cicero gave his means to Pompeius, he took money from Atticus' bailiff (vilicus) and borrowed from others.
Date: "at that time", when Cicero handed his means to Pompeius (48 BC, cf. Att. 11.3.3); the letter is of 47 BC.

Original Text:
46 atque ut eius impudentiam perspicere possitis, causam ipsam quae levissimi hominis animum in Flaccum incitavit, quaeso, cognoscite. fundum Cymaeum Romae mercatus est de pupillo Meculonio. Cum verbis se locupletem faceret, haberet nihil praeter illam impudentiam quam videtis, pecuniam sumpsit mutuam a Sex. Stloga, iudice hoc nostro, primario viro, qui et rem agnoscit neque hominem ignorat; qui tamen credidit P. Fulvi Nerati, lectissimi hominis, fide. ei cum solveret, sumpsit a C. M. Fufiis, equitibus Romanis, primariis viris. hic hercule cornici oculum, ut dicitur. nam hunc Hermippum, hominem eruditum, civem suum, cui debebat esse notissimus, percussit. eius enim fide sumpsit a Fufiis. securus Hermippus Temnum proficiscitur, cum iste se pecuniam quam huius fide sumpserat a discipulis suis diceret Fufiis persoluturum.
47 habebat enim rhetor iste discipulos quosdam locupletis,quos dimidio redderet stultiores quam acceperat; neminem tamen adeo infatuare potuit ut ei nummum ullum crederet. itaque cum Roma clam esset profectus multosque minutis mutuationibus fraudavisset, in Asiam venit Hermippoque percontanti de nomine Fufiano respondit se omnem pecuniam Fufiis persolvisse. interim, neque ita longo intervallo, libertus a Fufiis cum litteris ad Hermippum venit; pecunia petitur ab Hermippo. Hermippus ab Heraclida petit; ipse tamen Fufiis satis facit absentibus et fidem suam liberat; hunc aestuantem et tergiversantem iudicio ille persequitur. A recuperatoribus causa cognoscitur.
48 nolite existimare, iudices, non unam et eandem omnibus in locis esse fraudatorum et infitiatorum impudentiam. fecit eadem omnia quae nostri debitores solent; negavit sese omnino versuram ullam fecisse Romae; Fufiorum se adfirmavit numquam omnino nomen audisse; Hermippum vero ipsum, pudentissimum atque optimum virum, veterem amicum atque hospitem meum, splendidissimum atque ornatissimum civitatis suae, probris omnibus maledictisque vexat. sed cum se homo volubilis quadam praecipiti celeritate dicendi in illa oratione iactaret, repente testimoniis Fufiorum nominibusque recitatis homo audacissimus pertimuit, loquacissimus obmutuit. itaque recuperatores contra istum rem minime dubiam prima actione iudicaverunt. Cum iudicatum non faceret, addictus Hermippo et ab hoc ductus est.

English translation:
46 And so that you may see his shamelessness, please hear the cause itself which roused the mind of this most frivolous man against Flaccus. He bought a farm at Cyme at Rome from the ward Meculonius. Though he made himself rich in words, and had nothing but the shamelessness you see, he borrowed money from Sextus Stloga, a judge of ours here, a leading man, who both recognizes the matter and knows the man; who however lent it on the credit of Publius Fulvius Neratus, a most excellent man. To repay him, he borrowed from Gaius and Marcus Fufius, Roman knights, leading men. Here, by Hercules, he pecked out a crow's eye, as they say. For he struck at this Hermippus, a learned man, his own fellow citizen, to whom he must have been very well known; for on his credit he borrowed from the Fufii. Hermippus, free of care, sets out for Temnus, while that man said he would pay the Fufii the money which he had borrowed on Hermippus' credit out of his pupils.
47 For this rhetor had some rich pupils, whom he would return half as wise as he received them; yet he could make none of them so foolish as to lend him a single sesterce. So when he had left Rome secretly and had cheated many by small borrowings, he came to Asia, and to Hermippus' inquiry about the Fufian debt he answered that he had paid the Fufii all the money. Meanwhile, not long after, a freedman of the Fufii came to Hermippus with a letter; the money is demanded from Hermippus. Hermippus demands it from Heraclides; yet he himself satisfies the Fufii in their absence and frees his credit; he pursues this man, wavering and shuffling, in court. The case is heard before recuperators.
48 Do not think, judges, that the shamelessness of cheats and deniers is not one and the same everywhere. He did everything our debtors usually do; he denied that he had raised any loan at all at Rome; he declared that he had never heard the name of the Fufii at all; and Hermippus himself, a most modest and excellent man, an old friend and guest of mine, most distinguished and most respected in his city, he harasses with every insult and abuse. But as the glib man was throwing himself about in that speech with a headlong speed of talk, suddenly, when the testimonies and the accounts of the Fufii were read out, the boldest of men took fright, the most talkative fell silent. So the recuperators judged against him a by no means doubtful matter at the first hearing. When he did not pay the judgment, he was assigned to Hermippus and led away by him.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Heraclides of Temnus, a rhetor, borrowed at Rome from Sextus Stloga on the credit (fides) of Publius Fulvius Neratus; to repay him he borrowed from the Fufii.
Date: not stated; the year of the speech (59 BC); the loan was made some years earlier.
Place: at Rome (§§46, 48).

Cum verbis se locupletem faceret, haberet nihil praeter illam impudentiam quam videtis, pecuniam sumpsit mutuam a Sex. Stloga, iudice hoc nostro, primario viro, qui et rem agnoscit neque hominem ignorat; qui tamen credidit P. Fulvi Nerati, lectissimi hominis, fide. ei cum solveret, sumpsit a C. M. Fufiis, equitibus Romanis, primariis viris. hic hercule cornici oculum, ut dicitur. nam hunc Hermippum, hominem eruditum, civem suum, cui debebat esse notissimus, percussit. eius enim fide sumpsit a Fufiis. securus Hermippus Temnum proficiscitur, cum iste se pecuniam quam huius fide sumpserat a discipulis suis diceret Fufiis persoluturum.
47 habebat enim rhetor iste discipulos quosdam locupletis,quos dimidio redderet stultiores quam acceperat; neminem tamen adeo infatuare potuit ut ei nummum ullum crederet. itaque cum Roma clam esset profectus multosque minutis mutuationibus fraudavisset, in Asiam venit Hermippoque percontanti de nomine Fufiano respondit se omnem pecuniam Fufiis persolvisse. interim, neque ita longo intervallo, libertus a Fufiis cum litteris ad Hermippum venit; pecunia petitur ab Hermippo. Hermippus ab Heraclida petit; ipse tamen Fufiis satis facit absentibus et fidem suam liberat; hunc aestuantem et tergiversantem iudicio ille persequitur. A recuperatoribus causa cognoscitur.
48 nolite existimare, iudices, non unam et eandem omnibus in locis esse fraudatorum et infitiatorum impudentiam. fecit eadem omnia quae nostri debitores solent; negavit sese omnino versuram ullam fecisse Romae; Fufiorum se adfirmavit numquam omnino nomen audisse; Hermippum vero ipsum, pudentissimum atque optimum virum, veterem amicum atque hospitem meum, splendidissimum atque ornatissimum civitatis suae, probris omnibus maledictisque vexat. sed cum se homo volubilis quadam praecipiti celeritate dicendi in illa oratione iactaret, repente testimoniis Fufiorum nominibusque recitatis homo audacissimus pertimuit, loquacissimus obmutuit. itaque recuperatores contra istum rem minime dubiam prima actione iudicaverunt. Cum iudicatum non faceret, addictus Hermippo et ab hoc ductus est.

English translation:
46 And so that you may see his shamelessness, please hear the cause itself which roused the mind of this most frivolous man against Flaccus. He bought a farm at Cyme at Rome from the ward Meculonius. Though he made himself rich in words, and had nothing but the shamelessness you see, he borrowed money from Sextus Stloga, a judge of ours here, a leading man, who both recognizes the matter and knows the man; who however lent it on the credit of Publius Fulvius Neratus, a most excellent man. To repay him, he borrowed from Gaius and Marcus Fufius, Roman knights, leading men. Here, by Hercules, he pecked out a crow's eye, as they say. For he struck at this Hermippus, a learned man, his own fellow citizen, to whom he must have been very well known; for on his credit he borrowed from the Fufii. Hermippus, free of care, sets out for Temnus, while that man said he would pay the Fufii the money which he had borrowed on Hermippus' credit out of his pupils.
47 For this rhetor had some rich pupils, whom he would return half as wise as he received them; yet he could make none of them so foolish as to lend him a single sesterce. So when he had left Rome secretly and had cheated many by small borrowings, he came to Asia, and to Hermippus' inquiry about the Fufian debt he answered that he had paid the Fufii all the money. Meanwhile, not long after, a freedman of the Fufii came to Hermippus with a letter; the money is demanded from Hermippus. Hermippus demands it from Heraclides; yet he himself satisfies the Fufii in their absence and frees his credit; he pursues this man, wavering and shuffling, in court. The case is heard before recuperators.
48 Do not think, judges, that the shamelessness of cheats and deniers is not one and the same everywhere. He did everything our debtors usually do; he denied that he had raised any loan at all at Rome; he declared that he had never heard the name of the Fufii at all; and Hermippus himself, a most modest and excellent man, an old friend and guest of mine, most distinguished and most respected in his city, he harasses with every insult and abuse. But as the glib man was throwing himself about in that speech with a headlong speed of talk, suddenly, when the testimonies and the accounts of the Fufii were read out, the boldest of men took fright, the most talkative fell silent. So the recuperators judged against him a by no means doubtful matter at the first hearing. When he did not pay the judgment, he was assigned to Hermippus and led away by him.

51 venio ad Lysaniam eiusdem civitatis, peculiarem tuum, Deciane, testem; quem tu cum ephebum Temni cognosses, quia tum te nudus delectarat, semper nudum esse voluisti. abduxisti Temno Apollonidem; pecuniam adulescentulo grandi faenore, fiducia tamen accepta, occupavisti. hanc fiduciam commissam tibi dicis; tenes hodie ac possides. Eum tu testem spe recuperandi fundi paterni venire ad testimonium dicendum coegisti; qui quoniam testimonium nondum dixit, quidnam sit dicturus exspecto. Novi genus hominum, novi consuetudinem, novi libidinem. itaque, etsi teneo quid sit dicere paratus, nihil tamen contra disputabo prius quam dixerit. totum enim convertet atque alia finget. quam ob rem et ille servet quod paravit, et ego me ad id quod adtulerit integrum conservabo.

English translation:
51 I come to Lysanias of the same city, your special witness, Decianus; whom, when you knew him as an ephebe at Temnus, because he pleased you naked then, you wished always to be naked. You took him away from Temnus to Apollonis; you put out money to the young man at great interest, yet with a security (fiducia) received. This security you say was forfeited to you; you hold and possess it today. You compelled him to come as a witness to give evidence in the hope of recovering his father's farm; since he has not yet given his evidence, I wait to see what he will say. I know the kind of men, I know their habit, I know their caprice. So, although I know what he is ready to say, I shall not argue against it until he has spoken. For he will turn everything round and invent other things. Therefore let him keep what he has prepared, and I shall keep myself fresh for whatever he brings.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Decianus (the prosecutor's ally) took the young Lysanias of Temnus away from Temnus to Apollonis and lent him money at great interest, taking a fiducia on his father's farm, which he says was forfeited to him ("Apollonidem" is the town Apollonis, not a person).
Interest: "at great interest" (grandi faenore); no rate.
Date: not stated; the year of the speech (59 BC); the loan was made earlier.

29 quod cum Deiotarus religione sua castissime tueretur, quem unum habemus in orbe terrarum fidelissimum huic imperio atque amantissimum nostri nominis, Brogitaro, ut ante dixi, addictum pecunia tradidisti. atque hunc tamen Deiotarum saepe a senatu regali nomine dignum existimatum, clarissimorum imperatorum testimoniis ornatum, tu etiam regem appellari cum Brogitaro iubes. sed alter est rex iudicio senatus per nos, pecunia Brogitarus per te appellatus alterum putabo regem, si habuerit unde tibi solvat quod ei per syngrapham credidisti. nam cum multa regia sunt in Deiotaro tum illa maxime, quod tibi nummum nullum dedit, quod eam partem legis tuae quae congruebat cum iudicio senatus, ut ipse rex esset, non repudiavit, quod Pessinuntem per scelus a te violatum et sacerdote sacrisque spoliatum reciperavit, ut in pristina religione servaret, quod caerimonias ab omni vetustate acceptas a Brogitaro pollui non sinit, mavultque generum suum munere tuo quam illud fanum antiquitate religionis carere. sed ut ad haec haruspicum responsa redeam, ex quibus est primum de ludis, quis est qui id non totum in istius ludos praedictum et responsum esse fateatur?

English translation:
29 And though Deiotarus guarded this with the purest piety, the one man in the whole world we have most loyal to this empire and most devoted to our name, you handed it over, as I said before, to Brogitarus, who was bound to you by money. And yet this Deiotarus, often judged by the senate worthy of the royal name, honoured by the testimonies of the most famous generals, you also order to be called king together with Brogitarus. But the one is king by the judgment of the senate through us, Brogitarus is called king through you for money; I shall think the other a king if he has the means to repay you what you lent him by a bond. For while there is much that is royal in Deiotarus, this above all, that he gave you not a single sesterce, that he did not reject that part of your law which agreed with the judgment of the senate, that he himself should be king, that he recovered Pessinus, criminally violated by you and robbed of its priest and rites, to keep it in its ancient worship, that he does not allow ceremonies received from all antiquity to be polluted by Brogitarus, and prefers that his son-in-law lack your gift rather than that shrine lack the antiquity of its worship. But to return to these answers of the haruspices, of which the first is about the games, who is there who does not admit that it was entirely foretold and answered about this man's games?

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Clodius, who by his law of 58 BC made the Galatian Brogitarus king and gave him Pessinus, lent him money by a bond (syngrapha); Cicero doubts he can repay.
Date: between Clodius' law (58 BC) and the speech (56 BC).

Original text: Cicero, De haruspicum responso, ed. W. Peterson (Oxford 1909); Perseus Digital Library (canonical-latinLit), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

86 quid avaritiae, quae criminibus infinitis implicata est, summam nunc explicem? generatim ea quae maxime nota sunt dicam. nonne sestertium centiens et octogiens, quod quasi vasari nomine in venditione mei capitis ascripseras, ex aerario tibi attributum Romae in quaestu reliquisti? nonne, cum cc talenta tibi Apolloniatae Romae dedissent ne pecunias creditas solverent, ultro Fufidium, equitem Romanum, hominem ornatissimum, creditorem debitoribus suis addixisti? nonne, hiberna cum legato praefectoque tuo tradidisses, evertisti miseras funditus civitates, quae non solum bonis sunt exhaustae sed etiam nefarias libidinum contumelias turpitudinesque subierunt? qui modus tibi fuit frumenti aestimandi, qui honorarii? si quidem potest vi et metu extortum honorarium nominari. quod cum peraeque omnes, tum acerbissime Bottiaei, Byzantii, Cherronensus, Thessalonica sensit. Vnus tu dominus, unus aestimator, unus venditor tota in provincia per triennium frumenti omnis fuisti.

English translation:
86 Why should I now unfold the sum of your avarice, which is entangled in countless crimes? I shall speak in general of the best-known things. Did you not leave at Rome, out at interest, the 18,000,000 sesterces assigned to you from the treasury, which you had entered as if for equipment in the sale of my life? When the Apolloniates had given you 200 talents at Rome so that they should not repay the money lent to them, did you not go further and hand over Fufidius, a Roman knight, a most distinguished man, the creditor, to his own debtors? When you had handed over the winter quarters to your legate and prefect, did you not utterly ruin wretched cities, which were not only drained of their goods but also suffered unspeakable outrages of lust and shame? What limit did you set to valuing grain, or to the gift of honour, if what is extorted by force and fear can be called a gift of honour? This all felt alike, but most bitterly the Bottiaeans, the Byzantines, the Chersonese, Thessalonica. You alone were master, assessor and seller of all the grain in the whole province for three years.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
The people of Apollonia owed money lent to them by Fufidius, a Roman knight; they paid Piso 200 talents at Rome not to repay it, and Piso handed the creditor over to his debtors.
Date: not stated; the year of the speech (55 BC); the loan was made before Piso's governorship of Macedonia (57-55 BC).

Original text: Cicero, In L. Calpurnium Pisonem, ed. A. C. Clark (Oxford 1909); Perseus Digital Library (canonical-latinLit), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

4 hoc ille natus, quamquam patrem suum numquam viderat, tamen et natura ipsa duce, quae plurimum valet, et adsiduis domesticorum sermonibus in paternae disciplinae similitudinem deductus est. multa gessit, multa contraxit, magnas partis habuit publicorum; credidit populis; in pluribus provinciis eius versata res est; dedit se etiam regibus; huic ipsi Alexandrino grandem iam antea pecuniam credidit; nec interea locupletare amicos umquam suos destitit, mittere in negotium, dare partis, augere re, fide sustentare. quid multa? cum magnitudine animi, tum liberalitate vitam patris et consuetudinem expresserat. pulsus interea regno Ptolomaeus dolosis consiliis, ut dixit Sibylla, sensit Postumus, Romam venit. cui egenti et roganti hic infelix pecuniam credidit, nec tum primum; nam regnanti crediderat absens; nec temere se credere putabat, quod erat nemini dubium quin is in regnum restitueretur a senatu populoque Romano.
5 in dando autem et credendo processit longius nec suam solum pecuniam credidit sed etiam amicorum, stulte; quis negat, aut quis iam audebit, quod male cecidit, bene consultum putare? sed est difficile, quod cum spe magna sis ingressus, id non exsequi usque ad extremum. supplex erat rex, multa rogabat, omnia pollicebatur, ut iam metuere Postumus cogeretur ne quod crediderat perderet, si credendi constituisset modum. nihil autem erat illo blandius, nihil hoc benignius, ut magis paeniteret coepisse quam liceret desistere.
6 hinc primum exoritur crimen illud; senatum corruptum esse dicunt. O di immortales! haec est illa exoptata iudiciorum severitas? corruptores nostri causam dicunt; nos qui corrupti sumus non dicimus? quid ergo? senatumne defendam hoc loco, iudices? omni equidem loco debeo; ita de me est meritus ille ordo; sed nec id agitur hoc tempore nec cum Postumi causa res ista coniuncta est. quamquam ad sumptum itineris, ad illam magnificentiam apparatus comitatumque regium suppeditata pecunia a Postumo est, factaeque syngraphae sunt in Albano Cn. Pompei, cum ille Roma profectus esset, tamen non debuit is qui dabat, cur ille qui accipiebat tum sumeret, quaerere. non enim latroni, sed regi credidit, nec regi inimico populi Romani, sed ei cuius reditum consuli commendatum a senatu videbat, nec ei regi qui alienus ab hoc imperio esset, sed ei quicum foedus feriri in Capitolio viderat.

English translation:
4 Born to this father, although he had never seen him, yet with nature itself as guide, which is most powerful, and through the constant talk of his household, he was led to the likeness of his father's way of life. He did much business, made many contracts, held large shares in the public contracts; he lent to peoples; his business was carried on in several provinces; he gave himself also to kings; to this very Alexandrian he had already before lent a large sum of money; nor meanwhile did he ever cease to enrich his friends, to send them into business, to give them shares, to increase their means, to support them with his credit. In short, in greatness of mind and in generosity he had copied the life and habits of his father. Meanwhile Ptolemaeus, driven from his kingdom by treacherous plots, as the Sibyl said, as Postumus found, came to Rome. To him, needy and asking, this unhappy man lent money, and not then for the first time; for he had lent to him while he reigned, though absent; nor did he think he was lending rashly, because no one doubted that he would be restored to his kingdom by the senate and the Roman people.
5 In giving and lending, however, he went further, and lent not only his own money but also that of his friends, foolishly; who denies it, or who will now dare to call well advised what has turned out badly? But it is hard not to pursue to the end what you have entered on with great hope. The king was a suppliant, asked much, promised everything, so that Postumus was now forced to fear losing what he had lent if he set a limit to lending. Nothing was more ingratiating than the king, nothing kinder than Postumus, so that he regretted having begun more than he could stop.
6 Hence first arises that charge: they say the senate was corrupted. O immortal gods! Is this that longed-for severity of the courts? Our corruptors are on trial; we who were corrupted are not? What then? Shall I defend the senate at this point, judges? I ought to in every place; that order has so deserved of me; but that is not the issue at this time, nor is that matter connected with Postumus' case. Although money for the cost of the journey, for that magnificence of equipment and the royal retinue, was supplied by Postumus, and bonds were made at Gnaeus Pompeius' Alban villa when the king had left Rome, yet he who gave ought not to have asked why he who received was then borrowing. For he lent not to a brigand but to a king, not to a king hostile to the Roman people, but to one whose restoration he saw commended to the consul by the senate, not to a king foreign to this empire, but to one with whom he had seen a treaty struck on the Capitol.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Rabirius Postumus had already lent the king a large sum while the king reigned, Rabirius being absent (§4: "regnanti crediderat absens"); the loans at Rome after the king's expulsion are the second row of this passage. Interest is mentioned in §39 ("induced by interest").
Date: before the king's expulsion (58 BC), during his reign (from 80 BC); the speech is of 54 BC.

Original text: Cicero, Pro C. Rabirio Postumo, ed. A. C. Clark (Oxford 1909); Perseus Digital Library (canonical-latinLit), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Source: Cic. Rab. Post. 4 (https://scaife.perseus.org/reader/urn:cts:latinLit:phi0474.phi030.perseus-lat2:4-6/)

Original Text:
12.12.2 Nam cum emere vellet in Palatio domum et pecuniam in praesens non haberet, a P. Sulla, qui tum reus erat, mutua sestertium viciens tacita accepit.
12.12.3 Ea res tamen, priusquam emeret, prodita est et in vulgus exivit, obiectumque ei est quod pecuniam domus emendae causa a reo accepisset.
12.12.4 Tum Cicero, inopinata obprobratione permotus, accepisse se negavit ac domum quoque se empturum negavit atque Adeo, inquit, verum sit accepisse me pecuniam, si domum emero. Sed cum postea emisset et hoc mendacium in senatu ei ab amicis obiceretur, risit satis atque inter ridendum: Ἀκοινονόητοι, inquit, homines estis, cum ignoratis prudentis et cauti patrisfamilias esse, quod emere velit empturum sese negare propter competitores emptionis.

English translation:
12.12.2 For when he wished to buy a house on the Palatine and did not have the money at hand, he secretly received from Publius Sulla, who was then on trial, a loan of 2,000,000 sesterces.
12.12.3 The matter, however, before he bought, was betrayed and became public, and he was charged with having received money from a defendant to buy a house.
12.12.4 Then Cicero, disturbed by the unexpected reproach, denied that he had received it and denied too that he would buy the house, and said, "So let it be true that I received the money, if I buy the house." But when he later bought it and this lie was thrown in his face in the senate by his friends, he laughed heartily and in the midst of his laughter said: "You are men without common sense, since you do not know that it is the part of a prudent and careful head of a household to deny that he will buy what he wishes to buy, because of competitors for the purchase."

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Cicero secretly borrowed 2,000,000 sesterces from Publius Sulla to buy a house on the Palatine.
Date: Sulla was "then on trial" (his trial of 62 BC, defended by Cicero).

9 Secutum est bellum gestum apud Mutinam. in quo si tantum eum. prudentem dicam, minus quam debeam praedicem, cum ille potius divinus fuerit, si divinatio appellanda est perpetua naturalis bonitas, quae nullis casibus agitatur neque minuitur. hostis Antonius iudicatus Italia cesserat: spes restituendi nulla erat. non solum inimici, qui tum erant potentissimi et plurimi, sed etiam qui adversariis eius se venditabant et in eo laedendo aliquam consecuturos sperabant commoditatem, Antonii familiares insequebantur, uxorem Fulviam omnibus rebus spoliare cupiebant, liberos etiam exstinguere parabant. Atticus, cum Ciceronis intima familiaritate uteretur, amicissimus esset Bruto, non modo nihil iis indulsit ad Antonium violandum, sed e contrario familiares eius ex urbe profugientes, quantum potuit, texit, quibus rebus indiguerunt, adiuvit. Publio vero Volumnio ea tribuit, ut plura a parente proficisci non potuerint. ipsi autem Fulviae, cum litibus distineretur magnisque terroribus vexaretur, tanta diligentia officium suum praestitit, ut nullum illa stiterit vadimonium sine Attico, Atticus sponsor omnium rerum fuerit. quin etiam, cum illa fundum secunda fortuna emisset in diem neque post calamitatem versuram facere potuisset, ille se interposuit pecuniamque sine faenore sineque ulla stipulatione credidit, maximum existimans quaestum, memorem gratumque cognosci, simulque aperiens se non fortunae, sed hominibus solere esse amicum. quae cum faciebat, nemo eum temporis causa facere poterat existimare: nemini enim in opinionem veniebat Antonium rerum potiturum. sed sensus eius a nonnullis optimatibus reprehendebatur, quod parum odisse malos cives videretur. ille autem, sui iudicii, potius quid se facere par esset intuebatur quam quid alii laudaturi forent.

English translation:
9 Then followed the war fought at Mutina. If in it I should call him only prudent, I should praise him less than I ought, since he was rather divine, if a constant natural goodness, which is shaken or lessened by no chances, is to be called divination. Antonius, declared a public enemy, had left Italy: there was no hope of his restoration. Not only his enemies, who were then most powerful and most numerous, but also those who offered themselves to his opponents and hoped to gain some advantage by injuring him, were pursuing Antonius' friends, wished to strip his wife Fulvia of everything, and were preparing even to put his children to death. Atticus, though he enjoyed the intimate friendship of Cicero and was a very close friend of Brutus, not only did not indulge them in harming Antonius, but on the contrary sheltered his friends, as far as he could, as they fled from the city, and helped them with whatever they needed. To Publius Volumnius he gave such help that more could not have come from a parent. And to Fulvia herself, when she was distracted by lawsuits and harassed by great terrors, he showed such diligent service that she appeared on no bail-day without Atticus, and Atticus was her surety in everything. Moreover, when in her prosperity she had bought an estate on credit and after her misfortune could not raise a loan, he stepped in and lent her the money without interest and without any stipulation, thinking it the greatest gain to be known as mindful and grateful, and at the same time showing that he was accustomed to be a friend to men, not to fortune. When he did this, no one could think he did it for the sake of the times: for it occurred to no one that Antonius would gain power. But his attitude was blamed by some of the optimates, because he seemed too little to hate bad citizens. He, however, of his own judgment, looked rather to what it was right for him to do than to what others would praise.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Fulvia, wife of Antonius, had bought an estate on credit and could not raise a loan after his defeat; Atticus lent her the money.
Interest: without interest and without stipulation (sine faenore sineque ulla stipulatione).
Date: after the war at Mutina, when Antonius had been declared a public enemy (43 BC).

English translation:
1 Chaeremon to Cronion, who manages the record office, greeting. A copy of the petition submitted to us is appended below. Please
2 act in accordance with what it sets out, as is proper. Farewell. Year twenty-three of Tiberius Caesar Augustus, Choiak third.
3 To Chaeremon, exegetes,
4 from Taorseus daughter of Eutychus, with her guardian, her kinsman Ptolemaeus son of Chaeremon. The man who lived with me,
5 Galates son of Lysimachus, died leaving by me three minor sons, Lysas and Lysimachus
6 and Eutychas, whose guardian I was registered through you. Whereas Galates, together with his brothers
7 Didymus the elder and Didymus the younger and Lysimachus, owed to Castor and Lysimachus, both sons of Lysimachus,
8 under a sequestration (mesiteia) completed in year 10 of Tiberius Caesar Augustus, on their ancestral
9 catoecic land, a catoecic allotment of eighty-two arouras in the Polemon division, of which
10 thirty-seven arouras are at Tebtunis in two parcels, twenty-five arouras at Theogonis in one parcel,
11 formerly of Lucius Terentius, and the remaining twenty arouras at Kerkesis in another parcel,
12 so that the arouras of the allotment are the aforesaid eighty-two or however many they are, the boundaries
13 of each parcel and the other details being set out in the said sequestration, for what was lent through it,
14 two talents and one thousand two hundred drachmas of silver of capital, and the interest accrued from the said
15 transaction up to now; and whereas Castor and Lysimachus have taken possession of the said
16 eighty-two arouras of the allotment, from the transfer they made in year 21 of Tiberius Caesar Augustus
17 through the registers of the catoeci, and have ceded part of it to their own
18 brothers: we therefore asked Castor and his brother Lysimachus to show us
19 kindness, on condition that we give them two thousand five hundred drachmas of silver in part payment of what
20 Galates and his brothers owe for public and private debts and other things, and that we all withdraw
21 and consent to the transfer made through the registers and to the cessions to the brothers
22 of Castor and his party. And I ask you to order that the manager of the record office be written to
23 to draw up with me, acting on behalf of my said minor sons
24 with myself as guardian, together with the brothers of Galates, Didymus
25 the elder and Didymus the younger and Lysimachus and Haryotes, the deed of withdrawal and consent
26 for the sixth share falling to my minor sons, the guarantee
27 following on me with the brothers of Galates as mutual sureties, so that I and the children may
28 be benefited. Read. Year 23 of Tiberius Caesar Augustus, Choiak 3. Farewell.

Loan in ll. 6-15: lent to Galates and his brothers (the two Didymi are "the elder" and "the younger") through a sequestration (mesiteia) on their catoecic allotment of 82 arouras; the document (AD 36) is the petition of Galates' widow Taorseus about the lenders' taking of the land.
Interest: interest-bearing, rate not stated.
Date: year 10 of Tiberius (= AD 23/24) (l. 8).
Place: not stated; the place of the document.

1 ⳨ To my good master, lover of Christ, lover of the poor, all-
2 renowned, most magnificent patrician and dux of the Thebaid
3 region, Apion, from Anoup, your wretched slave, from the
4 estate belonging to it called Phakra.
5 The glorious house of my good master possesses nothing unjust or impious,
6 but is always full of mercy, pouring out to the needy
7 what they need. Therefore I too, the wretched slave of my good master,
8 through this present petition wish to be shown mercy,
9 (and) to make known to your lordship that from my fathers and forefathers I have served
10 my good master, paying the public taxes every year; and by God's
11 will, in the past eleventh indiction and the past
12 tenth my animals died, and I borrowed no little gold,
13 (15 solidi), until I could buy the same animals. But when I approached
14 my good master and (asked him) to have mercy on me, (and) came here, the agents
15 of my master would not consent to act according to the order of my good
16 master. For if, master, your mercy does not reach me, I cannot stand
17 on my holding and be useful to the landowner's affairs. And
18 I beseech and implore your lordship to order that mercy be shown
19 to me, since I have come to great ruin. For I have no other
20 refuge but that of the Lord Christ and of your eminence.
21 And I will send up undying hymns to the Lord Christ for the
22 life of your lordship and of its most magnificent son
23 Strategius, master. ⳨

(recto)
1 In the year after the second consulship of Flavius Eusebius, vir clarissimus, Choiak 2, indiction 4, in Oxyrhynchus.
2 To Flavius Apphous, vir clarissimus, tribune, son of Eulogius of excellent memory,
3 of the splendid and most splendid city of the Oxyrhynchites, Aurelius Theon son of Ioannes,
4 his mother being Heraclia, pastry-cook, of the same city, greeting. I acknowledge by this
5 my written security that I have received from you as a loan, from hand
6 out of your house, for my own pressing need, two single imperial
7 gold solidi of full weight, in number two, total 2 gold solidi, on condition that I supply and
8 give to your nobility as interest on them until the term stated below
9 the lawful hundredth interest on them without default,
10 which interest and the capital itself I will of necessity repay to your excellence:
11 one solidus in the month of Tybi of the present year 172 (and) 141 of the
12 present fourth indiction, with the interest, and the other in the
13 month of Hathyr of the coming year [173] (and) 142 of the fifth indiction, with God's help,
14 with the interest, without delay and without any dispute, lawsuit
15 or judgment; and that I may not, when each term has come,
16 delay the repayment or ask for another extension,
17 or say that I have paid anything of this debt without written
18 receipts and a joint receipt, or before the return of this
19 document of mine, but you shall have the right of exaction upon me and upon
20 all my property. The document,
21 written in a single copy, is valid, and to the formal question I have assented. I, Aurelius Theon son of Ioannes, pas-
22 try-cook, the aforesaid, have received the two gold solidi of capital and will re-
23 pay them at the terms with the interest, and everything written is agreeable to me
24 as aforesaid, and to the formal question I have assented and released (it). I, Apphouas, lector,
25 son of Philoxenus, at his request wrote for him, as he does not know letters.
26 ☧ Written through me, Thoth (?). Choiak 2, indiction 4.
(verso)
27 (? lines illegible)

Interest: the lawful hundredth interest (νόμιμον ἑκατοστιαῖον τόκον, l. 9), i.e. 1% per month.
Term: one solidus in Tybi of the present year (= December AD 495/January AD 496), the other in Hathyr of the next (= October/November AD 496), each with interest (ll. 10-14).
Date: Choiak 2, indiction 4 (= 29 November AD 495).

8 [a copy is appended.] Helene daughter of Aphelix, grandson of Psosnaus, her mother being Eudaemonis, with her guardian, who is also surety for
9 the payment of everything under this mortgage, her own son Diodorus alias Longinus son of Amois,
10 grandson of Diodorus, of Chysis, to Spartas son of Pausanias, grandson of Sarapion, his mother being Didyme, of the city of Oxyrhynchus, greeting. I acknow-
11 ledge that I have from you, of silver of imperial coinage, one thousand eight hundred drachmas of capital, to which nothing at
12 all has been added, at interest of three obols per mina per month from the present month of Mecheir to the month of
13 Hathyr (?) of the coming 12th year, amounting to one hundred and eighty-nine drachmas, and the total of capital and inter-
14 est, one thousand nine hundred and eighty-nine drachmas of silver, (I have) on the mortgage of catoecic grain-bearing sown land,
15 full, in a rectangle, of four arouras of what belongs to me near the same Chysis in the Hermopolite, land
16 on release, in the kleros of Pausanias, of five arouras which are among twenty arouras held in common and undivided
17 with Chesphibis son of Petosiris and others, of all of which the neighbours are south a field, north the heirs of Saturninus
18 and others, east the boundary of the kleroi, west the same heirs of Saturninus; and the total of one thousand
19 nine hundred and eighty-nine drachmas of silver I will repay to you or your representatives on the thirtieth of Phaophi of the coming
20 [12th year] of Antoninus Caesar the lord, Armeniacus Medicus Parthicus Maximus, without any delay;
21 if I do not repay as written, you shall own in place of these (sums) the aforesaid arouras and may
22 use and manage them in whatever way you choose, and I am obliged to guarantee them to you as secure at
23 all times against everyone with every guarantee and free from cultivation of royal land and of your estate land and of anything
24 else from now on, and whenever you wish you may register a notice of possession of the mortgage and of the same arou-
25 ras through the property record office of the Hermopolite, without needing
26 my presence or co-signature. If I contravene any of this, it is to be invalid and I will pay in addition, for
27 each kind of contravention, the damages and a fine of six hundred drachmas of silver and to the trea-
28 sury the same, the aforesaid remaining valid nonetheless, and the mortgage is valid,
29 written in two copies, alike, without erasure or insertion, in the own hand of me, Diodorus alias Longinus.
30 Year 10 of Imperator Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus Medicus Parthicus Maximus,
31 Mecheir 24. I, Helene daughter of Aphelix, have from you, Spartas, the one thousand eight hundred drachmas at interest of three obols, amount-
32 ing to one hundred and eighty-nine drachmas, on the mortgage of the four arouras, and I will repay the
33 capital with the accrued interest on the thirtieth of Phaophi of the coming (12th) year; otherwise you shall own the same
34 arouras, and I will guarantee them as aforesaid. I, Diodorus alias Longinus son of Amois, am registered as my mother's guardian
35 and wrote for her as she does not know letters, and I am surety for the payment of what is due under the mortgage; the date is the same.

Interest: 3 obols per mina per month (l. 12), 189 drachmas in all to the term.
Term: until Phaophi 30 of the coming year 12 (= 28 October AD 171) (ll. 19-20).
Date: Mecheir 24, year 10 of Marcus Aurelius (= 18 February AD 170).
Place: not stated; the place of the document.

1 ⳨ In the year after the second consulship of our master Flavius Anastasius, the eternal
2 Augustus, Tybi 20, indiction 6, in the city of Oxyrhynchus.
3 To Flavius Didymus, the respected eparchicus, son of Timotheus of excellent memory,
4 of the splendid and most splendid city of the Oxyrhynchites, Aurelius
5 Theodorus, son of Megas alias Didymus of blessed memory, notary, of the
6 same city, signing below in my own hand, greeting. I acknowledge that I have received
7 from your reverence as a loan, from hand out of its house, for my own
8 and pressing need, single imperial gold solidi of full value,
9 six in number on the private standard of the Oxyrhynchites, less six carats, total 6 gold solidi less 6 carats,
10 which, being free from all risk, I will of necessity repay
11 to your excellence in the month of Pachon of the present year 174 (and) 143 of the
12 present sixth indiction, without delay. If, when the aforesaid
13 term has come, I [...] am negligent about the
14 said debt and you are willing to give me another (term) at our request, I acknowledge
15 that for the time running after the term I will supply the lawful hundredth
16 interest until full repayment of the same debt, which is to be repaid to you by me
17 after the term, if I so obtain [...], or the right of exaction being
18 yours upon me and upon all my property, which is pledged
19 for the payment of this debt by way of pledge and by right of mortgage. The document, written in a single copy,
20 is valid, and to the formal question I have assented. I, Aurelius Theodorus son of Megas, the aforesaid notary,
21 have received as capital six gold solidi less six carats and will repay them at the term,
22 and everything written is agreeable to me as aforesaid, and having signed with my own hand [...]
23 I, Aurelius Philoxenus, my mother being Heraeis, witness the document as aforesaid.
24 ☧ Written through me, Sarapammon.
(verso)
25 ⳨ Document of Theodorus, notary, of the (city) of the Oxyrhynchites, 6 gold solidi less 6 carats.

Term: in Pachon of the present year 174 (and) 143, indiction 6 (= April/May AD 498) (ll. 10-12); the lawful hundredth interest (1% per month) applies only after the term.
Date: Tybi 20, indiction 6 (= 15 January AD 498).

English translation:
1 In the consulship of our masters Valentinian and Valens,
2 eternal Augusti, Payni 14.
3 To the Aurelii Sarmates and Diogenes, riparii of the Oxyrhynchite,
4 from the Aurelii Dorotheus and Papnuthius, both sons of
5 Aphynchius, from the same city. Some time ago we were persuaded
6 by Eulogius, councillor, to fill the post of assistant
7 at the village of Teruthis and to provide every advance, to find
8 and give for the public dues of all kinds that were required, until
9 we should make the collection of the aforesaid village; and indeed, per-
10 suaded on these terms, we filled the post for him blamelessly.
11 But in the meantime he provided no advance, but handed us
12 over to the collectors, and with insults we were made to pay the dues
13 falling on the same village. Since, then, from great poverty, owning
14 nothing at all, we borrowed from moneylenders a stated quan-
15 tity of silver and of solidi, which were also given for the same public dues,
16 and since we were not allowed by the same Eulogius to go out to the afore-
17 said village from the month Tybi until the present, and we are paying interest
18 to the moneylenders who obliged us, not being allowed
19 to make the collection of what we advanced, but
20 he even sent his son Sarapion and Dorotheus, assistant, to Teru-
21 this in our place, and they have made the collection, for this reason we
22 submit the petition to your diligence, asking that the public
23 officials, who are also responsible, be summoned and compelled to
24 repay all that we advanced, so that we too may be able to repay
25 those who obliged us and remain in our own homes and not
26 for this cause become fugitives from our native place.

Loan in ll. 13-18: borrowed "a stated quantity of silver and of solidi" (the sum is not given) to pay the public dues of the village of Teruthis; the brothers are paying interest to the moneylenders; the document is their petition to the riparii. The same borrowing is mentioned in their petition P.Oxy. 48 3394.
Interest: interest-bearing, rate not stated.
Date: not stated; the year of the document (Payni 14, consulship of Valentinian and Valens = 8 June AD 365).
Place: not stated; the place of the document.

3.11.2 Indeed, when the philosophers had been banished from the city, I was with him at his house outside the city, and, what made it more conspicuous, that is more dangerous, I was praetor. Pliny lent the philosopher Artemidorus money to pay his debts, money Pliny himself had borrowed.
Interest: free of interest (gratuitam).

6.8.4 Iterum dices 'quorsus haec?' Debuit ei pecuniam Valerius Varus. Huius est heres Maximus noster, quem et ipse amo, sed Konjunktivs tu.
6.8.5 Rogo ergo, exigo etiam pro iure amicitiae, cures ut Atilio meo salva sit non sors modo verum etiam usura plurium annorum. Homo est alieni abstinentissimus sui diligens; nullis quaestibus sustinetur, nullus illi nisi ex frugalitate reditus.

English translation:
6.8.4 You will say again, "what is the point of this?" Valerius Varus owed him money. His heir is our Maximus, whom I too love, but you more closely.
6.8.5 I ask, then, I even demand by the right of friendship, that you see that my Atilius gets back safe not only the principal but also the interest of several years. He is a man most restrained from what belongs to others, careful of his own; he is supported by no gains, he has no income except from thrift.

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Valerius Varus owed Atilius Crescens money with the interest of several years; Pliny asks Priscus to see that Varus' heir Maximus repays principal and interest.
Interest: principal (sors) and interest (usura) of several years; no rate.
Date: not stated; the date of the letter (Book 6, c. AD 106-107); the loan was made several years earlier.
Konjunktivs (6.8.4) is so in the digital text; the editions read coniunctius ("more closely").

4.39.1 " Quare ergo," inquit, " Zeno vester, cum quingentos denarios cuidam mutuos promisisset et ipse illum parum idoneum comperisset, amicis suadentibus, ne daret, perseveravit credere, quia promiserat ?

English translation:
4.39.1 "Why then," he says, "did your Zeno, when he had promised a loan of five hundred denarii to a certain man and himself found him hardly sound, persist in lending, though his friends urged him not to give it, because he had promised?"

Literary source: the passage is cited by section; each line is one section.
Zeno, founder of the Stoic school, lent 500 denarii he had promised although friends warned him the borrower was unsound; the sum is given in Roman money by Seneca. The text gives no date.
